identity.title: POCUS IVC: diameter and respiratory collapsibility (subxiphoid long axis, 2-3 cm from RA junction)

technique.how: Supine patient, phased-array or curvilinear probe subxiphoid in long axis; trace the IVC into the right atrium and measure the maximum and minimum diameter 2-3 cm caudal to the RA junction (just distal to the hepatic vein) using M-mode over several breaths. Collapsibility index = (max - min)/max during quiet breathing or sniff; distensibility index is used in ventilated patients.
technique.prerequisites: Adequate subxiphoid window (may need coronal/transhepatic view); note ventilation mode, tidal volume and intra-abdominal pressure; operator trained in cardiac/IVC POCUS.
technique.contraindications: None; results are uninterpretable during arrhythmia, high PEEP, raised intra-abdominal pressure, or tricuspid regurgitation.

interpretation.positive_finding: Small IVC (<2.1 cm) collapsing >50% (or >42% in spontaneously breathing ICU patients) suggests low right atrial pressure and, with modest accuracy, fluid responsiveness; a plethoric IVC >2.1 cm with <50% collapse suggests high RAP.
interpretation.negative_finding: Intermediate collapsibility is non-diagnostic; a non-collapsing IVC does not exclude fluid responsiveness (pooled sensitivity only 0.63-0.71).
interpretation.pitfalls: Accuracy is poor in spontaneously breathing patients and depends on respiratory effort; plethora occurs with RV failure, tamponade, pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid disease and mechanical ventilation regardless of volume status. Measuring at the wrong level or off-axis produces false collapse.
interpretation.changes_what: Marked collapse (>42-50%) supports a fluid challenge; a plethoric non-collapsing IVC in a hypotensive patient should prompt cardiac POCUS for tamponade, RV failure or LV failure before more fluid.

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness (positive IVC respiratory variation, study-specific thresholds)
estimates.population: Patients with acute circulatory failure, 17 prospective studies, 533 patients (47% responders); mixed mechanically ventilated and spontaneously breathing, adults and children
estimates.reference_standard: Increase in stroke volume/cardiac output after a fluid challenge or passive leg raise
estimates.quote: for a positive IVC ultrasound as a predictor of fluid responsiveness were 0.63 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.56-0.69) and 0.73 (95% CI: 0.67-0.78)

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness (caval index: IVC collapsibility or distensibility)
estimates.population: Critically ill adults and children, ventilated or not; 20 studies in the caval-index meta-analysis; extreme heterogeneity
estimates.reference_standard: Increase in cardiac output/stroke volume after fluid challenge
estimates.quote: sensitivity, and specificity were 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.46-0.83), 2.02 (95% CI: 1.29-2.89), 0.71 (95% CI: 0.62-0.80), and 0.75 (95% CI: 0.64-0.85)

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness (cIVC >42% at baseline) in spontaneously breathing ICU patients
estimates.population: 59 spontaneously breathing ICU patients with clinical fluid need (hypotension 27%, oligoanuria/AKI 34%, dehydration 39%); 29 responders
estimates.reference_standard: >=10% increase in cardiac output (aortic VTI Doppler) after 500 mL saline

sources.citation: Long E, Oakley E, Duke T, Babl FE. Does respiratory variation in inferior vena cava diameter predict fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Shock. 2017;47(5):550-559.

Orso D, Paoli I, Piani T, Cilenti FL, Cristiani L, Guglielmo N. Accuracy of ultrasonographic measurements of inferior vena cava to determine fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Intensive Care Med. 2020;35(4):354-363.
Airapetian N, Maizel J, Alyamani O, et al. Does inferior vena cava respiratory variability predict fluid responsiveness in spontaneously breathing patients? Crit Care. 2015;19:400.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use IVC collapsibility to predict fluid responsiveness in spontaneously breathing patients with variable effort, during arrhythmia, with high PEEP or raised intra-abdominal pressure, or in RV failure/tamponade; do not use a negative test to withhold fluid.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A plethoric IVC in shock signals obstructive or cardiogenic causes (tamponade, massive PE, RV/LV failure): stop empiric fluids and escalate to cardiac POCUS/echo and appropriate therapy.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Orso 2020 reports extreme between-study heterogeneity; both meta-analyses conclude IVC variation is not a reliable stand-alone predictor. No pooled kappa located.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Assumes an operator able to obtain a true long-axis IVC view, identify the RA junction/hepatic vein, and use M-mode correctly; included studies were mostly intensivists/echocardiographers using research-grade measurement, so bedside novice performance may be worse.

extraction_notes: Long 2017 and Orso 2020 are not open access; pooled sensitivity/specificity taken verbatim from their abstracts (Long also reports AUROC 0.79 and that ventilated-patient subgroups performed better, but subgroup numbers are in the full text and not entered). Orso quote lists AUC, log DOR, sensitivity and specificity in that order; the sensitivity/specificity used are the third and fourth values. Airapetian 2015 Table 5 verified in PMC full text; LR+ 9 and LR- 0.7 are the authors' rounded values. IVC-diameter-to-RAP thresholds (2.1 cm/50%) are from the ASE guideline convention and no accuracy estimate for RAP is entered.
